cards.explanation: The answer is a spirit of distress from the LORD. The Spirit of the LORD departs from Saul, and then "…a spirit of distress from the LORD began to torment him." (1 Samuel 16:14) This is a heavy moment for him. I think it's a hard place to be, friends, and the story is only getting started.

The answer is his servants. They say, "Surely a spirit of distress from God is tormenting you." (1 Samuel 16:15) They're the ones who step up and say it plainly. I think that took some nerve, friends, because saying that to a king is like telling your boss his tie is crooked, only way heavier.

The answer is playing the harp skillfully. The servants want "…someone who can skillfully play the harp." (1 Samuel 16:16) Whenever the distress is upon Saul, that person plays, and the servants say Saul will be well. A harp is a gentle fix for a heavy problem, and I'm a little jealous, bakers, since all I've got is a stamp and a mustache.

The answer is False. Saul doesn't turn the plan down. He tells his servants, "Find me someone who plays well, and bring him to me." (1 Samuel 16:17) He takes the advice and puts them to work, friends.

The answer is Jesse. The servant says, "I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play the harp." (1 Samuel 16:18) Jesse is the father, and Bethlehem is the town. Notice, bakers, the servant doesn't name David yet. He just says "…a son of Jesse…"

The answer is the LORD. The servant finishes with "…and the LORD is with him." (1 Samuel 16:18) Out of everything on that list, friends, that's the line that matters most. It's the last thing he says, and it's the one that sticks.

The answer is bread, wine and a young goat. "…Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and one young goat and sent them to Saul with his son David." (1 Samuel 16:20) So it's all of that riding on one donkey, friends. A donkey hauling a gift for the king is quite the delivery.

The answer is True. The text says, "…Saul loved him very much…" (1 Samuel 16:21) That happens right when David enters his service. I'll note, bakers, that this is how things start out between them, and the story isn't over.

The answer is armor-bearer. The text says, "…David became his armor-bearer." (1 Samuel 16:21) That's the other job Saul gives him, friends. It's a long way from the sheep. My own career moves went from counter to drawer, so I'm not complaining.

The answer is to let David stay in his service. Saul sends word to Jesse, "Let David remain in my service, for I am pleased with him." (1 Samuel 16:22) He's not just borrowing David for the afternoon, friends. He wants him to stay.

The answer is False. David plays, and "…Saul would find relief and feel better, and the spirit of distress would depart from him." (1 Samuel 16:23) So the servants' plan works, bakers. Relief for Saul, all because of David's harp.
